question: Does Workday (NASDAQ: WDAY) report a gross or net retention metric in its annual or quarterly reporting? If so, provide the definition
answer:
Workday tracks and reports on Gross Revenue Retention Rate. 

The company defines Gross Revenue Retention Rate as the percentage of recurring revenue retained from existing customers and is calculated by taking total annual recurring revenue (“ARR”) of our customers as of the corresponding prior period-end and comparing that to ARR from that same set of customers as of the current period-end. The metric takes into account recurring revenues lost to product or customer churn but does not account for additional revenue earned from add-ons or net expansions, which include volume and price adjustments.

model_answer:
## Short answer

Yes — but only a **gross** retention metric. Workday discloses a **"gross revenue retention rate"** (GRR) in the MD&A of its Form 10-K and every Form 10-Q. It **stopped disclosing a net retention rate (NRR) in SEC filings** beginning with the FY2025 10-K (filed March 11, 2025), following SEC comment letters in 2024. Net retention now appears only in some older/occasional marketing materials (e.g., its 2023 Financial Analyst Day), not in current periodic reports.

---

## 1. The definition (verbatim, FY2026 10-K, Item 7 MD&A)

> "Our growth in subscription services revenues attributable to existing customers is further reflected by our gross revenue retention rate of approximately 97% as of January 31, 2026. **Our gross revenue retention rate measures the percentage of recurring revenue retained from existing customers and is calculated by taking total annual recurring revenue ("ARR") of our customers as of the corresponding prior period-end and comparing that to ARR from that same set of customers as of the current period-end.** The metric takes into account recurring revenues lost to product or customer churn but does not account for additional revenue earned from add-ons or net expansions, which include volume and price adjustments. Our high gross revenue retention rate demonstrates our ability to maintain our existing customer base and drive strong overall customer satisfaction.
>
> Our gross revenue retention rate is based on ARR, which represents the annualized value of active subscription contracts as of the end of each period. Each subscription contract is annualized by dividing the total contract value by the number of days in the contract term and then multiplying by 365. We exclude certain subscription contracts from the calculation, including contracts with terms less than one year that are distinct from our core product offering, such as contracts for tenants which are used for implementation and testing. To the extent that we are negotiating a renewal with a customer after the expiration of the subscription, ARR is only adjusted if the customer churns. We calculate ARR on a constant currency basis using exchange rates set at the beginning of each fiscal year."

Key mechanics:
- **Cohort-based:** same customer set measured at prior period-end ARR vs. current period-end ARR — no credit for price/volume expansion or cross-sell.
- **ARR-based, not GAAP revenue**, and constant-currency (frozen at start-of-fiscal-year FX rates).
- **Excludes** short-term contracts distinct from the core offering (e.g., implementation/testing tenants).
- Renewals under negotiation are **not** trued up until signed or the customer churns (so churn can lag).
- ARR is a **non-GAAP** measure; Workday has also told the SEC it does **not** consider GRR/NRR to be "key performance indicators" it manages the business by.

## 2. What it currently reports

| Period end | Gross revenue retention |
|---|---|
| Jan 31, 2026 (FY2026 10-K) | ~97% |
| Jul 31, 2026 (Q2 FY2027 10-Q) | ~97% |
| Jan 31, 2025 (FY2025 10-K) | ~98% |
| FY2024 and earlier | Only a floor: "exceeded 95%" (no figure) |

## 3. The net retention history — why it disappeared

- Through the FY2024 10-K and 2024 10-Qs, Workday said only that **gross retention "exceeded 95%" and net retention "exceeded 100%"** — both floors, no actual figures.
- In Aug–Sep 2024 SEC correspondence, the staff pushed back, noting the ">100%" net-retention statement may not reflect current rates and asking for the actual figures and same-cohort clarification. Workday's Sept 19, 2024 response:
  > "…we no longer intend to include disclosure related to net revenue retention rates in our SEC filings… We believe that the net revenue retention rate is largely duplicative of the change in revenue from existing customers as a measure of our business performance. As gross revenue retention provides insight into the recurring revenue retained from our existing customers, we currently intend to continue disclosing our gross revenue retention rate in future filings… we plan to disclose the actual, then-current gross revenue retention rate for each period."
- **Replacement disclosure:** Workday now decomposes subscription revenue growth by source — e.g., FY2026: "**Approximately 60% of the increase in subscription services revenues was attributable to expansion within our customers that existed as of the beginning of the comparable prior year period, and the remaining 40% was attributable to customers added after the beginning of the comparable prior year period.**" This is effectively where the expansion signal (the "net" side of NRR) now lives.
- Note the definition was also **reworded** in the FY2025 10-K (from the older "current period-end ARR of customers we retained year-over-year… divided by total ARR at the end of the corresponding prior period") to make explicit that GRR is computed on an identical customer cohort.

## 4. Caveats for users of the metric

- **Rounding:** "approximately 97%" is a whole-percent approximation, so a 1pt move (98% → 97%) may be within rounding.
- **Not comparable to peers' NRR:** Workday gives you *only* the downside (churn/contraction). Combined with the 60/40 growth split, you can approximate gross expansion, but not a true dollar-based NRR.
- **Investor materials still reference NRR** in places (2023 Financial Analyst Day: "Average Gross Revenue Retention 98%, Net Revenue Retention 100%+"; where NRR was defined as total ARR retention from existing customers on a TTM basis including add-ons, expansion, contraction and churn, excluding new customers). Treat old "100%+" claims as stale — the SEC correspondence implies actual NRR had drifted toward/below that level.
- **GRR ≠ revenue retention in GAAP terms:** it's ARR-based, excludes certain contracts, and uses frozen FX.

**Sources:** FY2026 Form 10-K (filed 3/6/2026) MD&A; FY2026 Q2 Form 10-Q for period ended 7/31/2026 (filed 8/27/2026) MD&A; FY2025 Form 10-K (filed 3/11/2025); Workday SEC correspondence filed 9/4/2024 and 9/19/2024 (File No. 001-35680); Workday 2023 Financial Analyst Day deck.
judge_reason: Correctly identifies Workday's Gross Revenue Retention Rate and provides a substantively identical definition covering all rubric elements.
